subtype: Approach: asking for help the moment a problem is stuck [Revision]
passage: I'm Bhavna, and my brother Pranav was doing fractions at the table last evening. He frowned at one question for a long time. About fifteen minutes passed, and he rubbed his eye and his pencil pressed harder. Then he stopped and drew a star beside the question. I don't know what he was thinking, but he closed his eyes for a moment. He walked over to our mother and said, "Amma, I'm stuck on this one." She sat with him for a few minutes. He went back to the other questions and finished them all.

qa.q: What did Pranav draw beside the question that he could not do?
qa.a: He drew a star beside it.

qa.q: What might Pranav have been feeling before he drew the star?
qa.a: He was probably frustrated and upset, since the question kept beating him. Bhavna saw that his pencil pressed harder and he rubbed his eye.

qa.q: What alternative approach could Pranav try, and why?
qa.a: He could look back at a solved example in his notebook before asking. It may show him the step he missed.

qa.q: How does Bhavna see the moment Pranav asked for help?
qa.a: Bhavna could only watch, and saw him stop, close his eyes, and choose to ask. Bhavna does not know what Pranav felt, but he got back to the other questions.

grounding: A child stuck on a fractions question notices he is only getting upset, marks it with a star, asks his mother and moves on to the other questions.

subtype: Approach: asking for help the moment a problem is stuck [Revision]
passage:
Monday. Tejas spent the whole evening on one fractions question, rubbing out until the page tore. Four other sums never got done, and he went to bed cross.
Wednesday. Another fractions question: 3/4 of 20. Fifteen minutes passed. Tejas noticed his fists were clenched and he was only getting angrier, not closer. He drew a star beside it, walked to the kitchen and said, "Aai, can you look at the starred one?" Then he went back and did the rest.
Friday. When a question stuck, he starred it after a few tries, asked Aai, and was downstairs playing with Divyansh by six.

qa.q: What happened to the page on Monday?
qa.a: He rubbed out until the page tore.

qa.q: How was Tejas feeling after fifteen minutes on Wednesday?
qa.a: He noticed his clenched fists and that he was only getting angrier, not closer, which told him to stop and ask.

qa.q: Which choice made the biggest difference, and why?
qa.a: Starring the question and asking Aai, then moving on; the other sums got done instead of one question eating the whole evening 👍

qa.q: How might Divyansh notice the change by Friday?
qa.a: Divyansh gets a playmate downstairs by six, instead of Tejas stuck indoors and cross.

grounding: Shows a boy noticing that fifteen minutes on a fractions question is only making him upset, starring it, asking his mother and doing the rest.

subtype: Approach: asking for help the moment a problem is stuck [Revision]
passage: Darshan, you've been glaring at that sum for twenty minutes. Let your Pankaj Chacha tell you something. When I was in Class 5, there was one fractions question I could not crack. I sat for fifteen minutes, pencil going round and round, and I noticed I wasn't thinking any more, only getting hot in the face. So I drew a star beside it, like our teacher did on the board for hard ones, and took it to my mother, who was stitching blouses by the window. She showed me in two minutes. And while she threaded her needle again, I did the other six questions. That star saved my evening.

qa.q: What was Pankaj's mother doing when he took the sum to her?
qa.a: She was stitching blouses by the window.

qa.q: What did young Pankaj notice about how he felt after fifteen minutes?
qa.a: He noticed he wasn't thinking any more, only getting hot in the face, which meant he was frustrated and upset.

qa.q: What was the turning point in the story, and why did it help?
qa.a: Drawing a star and asking his mother instead of staring; she explained it in two minutes and he could finish the other six.

qa.q: How might Pankaj's mother have seen being asked?
qa.a: She showed him in two minutes and went back to her needle, so she probably saw it as a small, easy interruption.

grounding: Illustrates a boy who notices fifteen minutes stuck is only upsetting him, stars the question, asks his mother and carries on.
